verdicts.rewritten_summary: Under the Penal Code in force since November 2012 same-sex conduct is legal with an equal age of consent of 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Labour Code (2019) Article 16.2 bans workplace discrimination on sexual orientation, and Penal Code Article 130(2)(d) allows enhanced sentencing for crimes motivated by sexual-orientation hatred. No same-sex marriages, civil unions or partnerships are recognised; a 2016 poll found 46% of Sao Tomeans would not mind an LGBTQ neighbour.

Wikipedia-derived page updated 25 Apr 2026: same-sex conduct legal since the November 2012 Penal Code with equal age of consent 16; no recognition of same-sex marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. The page lists no general anti-discrimination protection (the 2019 Labour Code employment ban is not reflected here) and records the country among UN Joint Statement signatories on sexual orientation and gender identity.

Country overview updated 12 Mar 2026: same-sex relations legal for men and women nationwide; legal gender recognition NOT possible; LGBTI organisations CAN register. Constitution Article 8.2's 'any other status' clause is read by the government as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity despite no explicit statutory protection.

Civil-society report of July 2024 (Projekta Foundation with VIDS and LGBT Platform): Constitution Article 8 covers SOGI only implicitly through 'any other status', and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since 1869. The LGBT Platform Suriname, founded 29 August 2011, unites PAREA, New Monday Foundation, Suriname Men United, Women's Way and Trans in Action; the report urges a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

Submission to the UN Human Rights Committee (115th session) from LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata: despite constitutional protection LGBTI persons still face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatization. It records that in March 2015 Penal Code Articles 175, 175a and 176 were revised to cover discrimination and hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation.

Human Rights Committee review of Suriname, July 2024: the State asserted its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, backed by monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission, while experts pressed on implementing the Inter-American Court's judgment on transgender identity. The Committee welcomed abolition of the death penalty in the Penal Code (2015) and Military Code (2021).

UN UPR pre-session summary of March 2016 from the Suriname LGBT Platform: since the 2011 UPR the State revised the penal code to equalise the age of consent for same- and opposite-sex conduct and to add sexual-orientation discrimination provisions. The platform also reports it has been excluded from state consultative processes despite repeated requests.

Wikipedia timeline of the 12 October 2022 Bratislava shooting: a 19-year-old attacker whose primary target was then-prime minister Eduard Heger (the LGBT bar Teplaren was 'plan B') arrived about 18:35 and at 19:11 fired eight shots at Teplaren, killing two and injuring one. The article's investigation, victims and perpetrator sections document the planning, the LGBT-venue target and the aftermath.

Feature of 7 February 2023: Slovakia's trans community remains precarious after the 12 October 2022 terrorist attack on the Bratislava LGBT bar, which rights groups say 'marked a new era' for trans people in the country. Existing transition rules already required surgical sterilisation before changing documents, and the aftermath brought even greater fears about the future.

Country overview updated 12 Mar 2026: Slovenia is regarded as among the most progressive countries in Central and Eastern Europe on LGBTIQ rights - same-sex relations legal nationwide, legal gender recognition possible, LGBTI organisations registerable - with comprehensive antidiscrimination laws enacted since 2016 explicitly covering sexual orientation and gender identity.

Ministry of the Interior notice of 29 October 2022: the local-jurisdiction step in legal gender-change procedures was abolished on the recommendation of the Advocate of the Principle of Equality, so transgender persons are no longer exposed to involuntary disclosure of transgender identity in their local environment.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): Legebitra documented 17 cases of bias-motivated speech and TransAkcija documented 25 cases of direct bias-motivated incidents in 2023. After Pride, LGBTIQ+ organisations held a press conference about attacks and rising hate while the Prime Minister took three days to react and the Interior Minister made no statements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): the Health Ministry officially confirmed to the Interdisciplinary Council for Gender Recognition that medical treatment is not required for legal gender recognition and formally asked the Interior Ministry to amend the relevant Civil Registry Act sub-article. The review also notes the death at 73 of a founder of Slovenia's grassroots LGBTI movement.

US State Department 2023 report on Slovenia: no laws criminalise consensual same-sex conduct and there were no reports of state-condoned violence, but authorities recorded violence incidents without tracking case numbers and local NGOs called violence against LGBTQI+ persons prevalent and under-reported. In June 2023 a woman wearing a rainbow flag was assaulted near the Ljubljana Pride route, marchers had eggs thrown at them and rainbow flags were burned on video.

ENACT national report of January 2025 (EU CERV-2023 project): civil society provides LGBTI hate-crime victims counselling, advocacy and safe spaces, but LGBTI persons using generic victim-support services face heteronormative hurdles. The report documents institutional shortcomings in the anti-LGBTI hate-crime framework.

UPI report of 25 July 2006: Slovenia passed a law legalising same-sex marriage but restricted the ceremony to the two partners plus a local community registration official - no friends or relatives. Gay and lesbian organisations welcomed the move as a concrete step while criticising the law as 'insufficient'.

TGEU report of 16 July 2025: Sweden's new Legal Gender Recognition Act came into force on 1 July 2025, simplifying the procedure but falling short of a full self-determination model, with medical barriers remaining.

Swedish-language SVT report of October 2025: swimming-pool giant Medley stops trans people from choosing changing rooms - the article explains why trans customers may no longer pick changing facilities at the chain, a direct everyday-facility access setback documented for trans visitors.

Brå (National Council for Crime Prevention) report 2024:13: supplements Swedish hate-crime statistics with a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences where police identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives - the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025): a bill would extend protection of victims of conversion practices when carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure. In November the Church of Sweden decided new priests must be willing to marry same-sex couples, passing 141 votes at the 2025 Church Council.

Open-access article in Sexuality Research and Social Policy (4 February 2016, vol 13, pp 119-129): traces LGBT policy development in Sweden's military from 1944 to 2014 - the historical record behind current service conditions.

2019 edition of the Spartacus Gay Travel Index reported by Newsweek: Canada, Portugal and Sweden tied as the most LGBT-friendly travel destinations - third-party evidence on Sweden's standing as a visitor destination.

TT/The Local, 28 January 2017: Sweden's main national board decided transgender people will no longer be classified as 'mentally ill', the depathologisation step for trans residents' diagnostic status.
Country overview updated 12 March 2026: same-sex relations ILLEGAL for men and women throughout Eswatini; legal gender recognition NOT possible; LGBTI organisations NOT able to register.
Freedom in the World 2024: Eswatini rated Not Free with an overall score of 17/100 (Political Rights 1/40, Civil Liberties 16/60) - an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space.

BTI 2024 country report: the government denies LGBTQ+ groups the ability to register as organisations, within a wider pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment under an oppressive environment ('Mswati must fall' having become a common protest slogan).

US State Department 2021 report on Eswatini: some traditional, religious and government officials criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In June, LGBTQI+ persons conducted a virtual Pride celebration without incident.
Swazi Media Commentary of December 2018: a church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened - religious-space inclusion documented alongside 'no let-up on discrimination in the kingdom'.

MambaOnline, July 2018: the first eSwatini Pride was declared a 'perfect success' - the inaugural Pride in the kingdom, marking public LGBT visibility in a state where same-sex conduct remains illegal.
MambaOnline, July 2019: Eswatini's registrar of companies refused to register an LGBTI group - the documented administrative blocking of organisational recognition in the kingdom.

Cornell Law gender-justice page: under the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) Section 5, protected characteristics now include sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status, giving an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences. The Constitution separately guarantees freedom from torture (Art 16) and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex (Art 27).

PinkNews, 18 May 2016: Seychelles repealed colonial-era Penal Code Section 151, which had allowed up to 14 years' imprisonment for male same-sex sex - framed as the popular holiday destination 'opening its arms to LGBT people'.

Travel guide: notes the 2016 decriminalisation of same-sex acts as a significant victory for the islands, while advising both local residents and tourists to stay vigilant and informed about the current legal and social landscape - practical visitor guidance for the destination.

Erasing 76 Crimes, 27 September 2024: a newly revised law calls for increased prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward victims' sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability - per the Human Dignity Trust, after South Africa Seychelles is only the second African country to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation. Before 2016 the penal code punished male same-sex intimacy with up to 14 years.

GEM (Guardians of the Gem) report of April 2025 on LGBTQIA individuals in Syria after the fall: working through an on-the-ground reporter network, the organisation investigated and found inaccurate a report claiming LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted and targeted in Homs, debunking it to avoid stirring incitement against the community.

Country overview updated 12 March 2026: Syria's legal landscape remains highly restrictive - Penal Code Articles 520 ('acts against nature') and 517 (public indecency) criminalise same-sex conduct for both men and women; legal gender recognition impossible; LGBTI organisations cannot register.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021): documents LGBT activism across the Middle East and North Africa including Syria, with tallies that ISIS claimed at least 16 killings in Syria for alleged sodomy as of June 2016 (23 in Iraq, 3 in Libya). Activists worked to draw attention to the killings including at the UN Security Council.

Syria Direct feature of 11 October 2020 (Will Christou, Alicia Medina): LGBT Syrians describe life at home and abroad - in Damascus homosexuality and 'public decency' offences are illegal, and a 36-year-old (Amira al-Tabbaa) describes living 'only in whispers' when meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes.

Newsweek, 2015: two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever meeting on LGBT rights at the UN Security Council - a closed session co-sponsored by the US and Chile - about the constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.

PinkNews, 23 June 2010: Syrian authorities raided several private gay parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men in the latest swoop - most charged with 'homosexual acts', others with dealing or buying drugs, per gaymiddleeast.com.
